claims.text: In tungsten-based refractory alloys at high temperature, plastic strain is primarily governed by vacancy diffusion-driven dislocation climb.
In tungsten-based refractory alloys at high temperature, toughness is primarily governed by vacancy diffusion-driven dislocation climb.
Adding an alloying element that retards vacancy diffusion will inhibit dislocation climb.
Inhibiting dislocation climb will suppress dynamic recovery.
Suppressing dislocation climb and dynamic recovery will increase work hardening.
Suppressing dislocation climb and dynamic recovery will increase fracture toughness.
Retarding vacancy diffusion will reduce overall high-temperature plastic strain.
Vacancy density and mobility mediate dislocation climb.
At elevated temperatures, vacancy diffusion facilitates dislocation climb.
Dislocation climb enables dynamic recovery and greater plastic strain.
Limiting dislocation climb causes a buildup of dislocations.
The modified alloy should show a statistically significant increase in work hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy should show a statistically significant increase in fracture toughness relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy should show reduced overall plastic strain capacity relative to the unmodified alloy.
Vacancy diffusion-driven dislocation climb is expected to dominate in the unmodified tungsten-based alloy under the specified high-temperature conditions.
The proposed mechanism should operate approximately between 1000°C and 1500°C, where vacancy diffusion is thermally activated.
At lower temperatures, dislocation glide predominates and the proposed climb-controlled mechanism may not apply.
